title: How To Deal With A Principal Who Doesn't Say Hello
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin addresses the unsettling experience of a principal who walks past staff without any acknowledgment, which can leave teachers questioning their standing or reputation. While he calls such behavior rude and unprofessional, he reassures readers that it is almost never personal—principals who behave this way are usually overwhelmed and avoiding interactions that might create more work for them. He warns, however, that the behavior is a legitimate red flag about a principal's leadership and interpersonal skills, since staff morale depends on basic courtesies like greetings. His advice is to never let the snub affect one's self-worth, to interact with such principals only when necessary, and to remain kind and professional while withholding an unprompted hello until the principal offers one first. He closes with the observation that confidence and a focus on one's own work tend to eventually earn even the most oblivious administrator's respect.
points: A principal who ignores greetings is usually overwhelmed and avoiding interaction, not sending a personal message.
Such behavior nonetheless signals real leadership weaknesses, since staff morale depends on basic courtesies.
The recommended response is to keep the relationship strictly professional and need-to-know only.
Teachers should wait for the principal to initiate a greeting rather than offering one unprompted every time.
Confidence in one's own work, detached from the need for administrative approval, tends to earn respect over time.
quotes: Now, before we go any further, I want to say that such behavior is beyond the pale. It’s rude and unprofessional and there’s no excuse for it. But here’s the thing: It’s not about you.
They’re just overwhelmed. They’re so far underwater and lost in thought that you don’t even register.
But the biggest red flag is that they don’t see the value in greeting staff members, however brief—which is a clear sign of poor leadership.

Namely, interact with them only out of necessity, which if you do your job should be a rare occurrence. Be kind. Be accommodating. But keep the relationship utmost professional, need to know basis only.
When you’re confident in your own skin, when you know you’re doing right by your students and don’t need anyone’s approval, people tend to bend over backwards to give it to you anyway.
